# The Real Risks of Cleaning an Oil-Saturated Alternator

An alternator that won't charge isn't a software bug; it's a hardware failure caused by physical contamination or internal component degradation. When you encounter a scenario where power steering pump sludge has coated the unit, the immediate instinct is to clean it and hope for a restoration of function. However, from an engineering standpoint, the decision to clean versus replace depends entirely on what has actually happened inside the casing.

The primary concern with oil or grease contamination is not merely aesthetic; it is electrical. Alternators rely on slip rings to transfer high-voltage DC power from the stationary stator to the rotating rotor. If a viscous sludge like power steering fluid coats these slip rings, it creates an unintended load path. When the engine spins, this conductive sludge can cause arcing across the slip ring surface. Over time, this electrical resistance generates localized heat, which burns off the carbon brush material and eventually destroys the rotor windings.

Simply wiping the exterior with a solvent or degreaser does not address this internal damage. If the sludge has already caused the brushes to wear down past their minimum length or if the slip rings are pitted from arcing, cleaning the exterior will not restore charging capability. The alternator may spin freely and look pristine after a wash, but it will fail to generate voltage as soon as the load is applied.

Before attempting any cleaning procedure, you must inspect the internal components. Remove the unit from the vehicle and open the rear cover. Check the condition of the carbon brushes. If they are below 1/4 inch in length or unevenly worn, replacement is mandatory regardless of how clean the exterior looks. Similarly, examine the slip rings for deep grooves or discoloration indicating thermal damage. If you find significant pitting, a light file can smooth minor imperfections, but severe scoring requires a new unit.

If the internal components are still in good condition, a cleaning process is technically feasible. The goal is to remove the dielectric barrier of the sludge without introducing new contaminants. Start by removing all external wiring and belts. Use an electrical contact cleaner or a mixture of acetone and a soft brush to agitate the sludge on the slip rings and exterior housing. Avoid high-pressure water jets, as they can force oil past the rear bearing seal.

After cleaning, you must dry the unit thoroughly. Compressed air is ideal for blowing out moisture from the ventilation slots and around the bearings. Reinstalling a wet alternator risks immediate hydro-lock in the bearings or short-circuiting of the internal windings once it cools down. Once dry, reinstall the brushes if they are new, ensuring the tensioner spring provides adequate pressure against the slip rings.

Finally, perform a load test. Do not rely on a multimeter check at idle speed; run the engine at 2,000 RPM and measure the output voltage at the battery terminals with the headlights and AC on. If the voltage rises above 13.5V under load, the cleaning was successful. If it remains below 13V or fluctuates wildly, the internal damage from the sludge is irreversible, and replacement is the only viable option to prevent a complete electrical system failure.
